newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition says West can help end Serbian crisis.
newsitem.headline: Opposition says West can help end Serbian crisis.

text.p: With its legal and administrative options exhausted, Yugoslavia's opposition coalition has turned to international pressure to help resolve the crisis over its allegations of election fraud.

On Tuesday the opposition coalition Zajedno (Together) lost a legal battle for control of Belgrade's urban government when the Yugoslav federal supreme court refused to hear its claims of election fraud by the ruling socialists.
As more than 100,000 Zajedno supporters demonstrated in the city, electoral commission chief Radomir Lazarevic said "all legal remedies were exhausted" as a result of the decision.

The opposition also boycotted the opening session of the Yugoslav parliament on Tuesday, declaring it would not sit in the newly elected body until the Serbian government accepts Zajedno victories in last month's local elections.

With no legal avenues remaining, the federal parliamentary boycott underway and the Serbian state assembly in recess while the authorities "fumigate" the building, Zajedno was running out of new levers to pull in its three-week old campaign.
But one opposition leader, Zoran Djindjic, told Reuters he believed Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic was still sensitive to the growing barrage of Western criticism.
"The only thing Milosevic cares about is international pressure, and it is for certain that in the next few days he will attempt to find a political solution," Djindjic said.

While the opposition vowed to maintain its daily demonstrations demanding the ouster of Milosevic, Yugoslav Federal Interior Minister Vukasin Jokanovic warned of a possible crackdown. "Demonstrations will be crushed if protesters use force," he told Reuters.
But while Jokanovic waved the stick, another member of Milosevic's camp hinted a carrot may be available.
The Yugoslav United Left (JUL), in coalition with the Socialists in federal government, said a "common solution" was possible.
JUL president Ljubisa Ristic told the independent news agency Beta that "readiness for talks and agreements will mature slowly."

"In politics...there is a need to come to a solution so I believe that such a common solution will be reached however difficult, ugly, unpleasant and dramatic the situation may now seem," Ristic said.
Political analysts said the statement appeared to be an attempt to guage the opposition's willingness to negotiate for a political solution.
But Ristic also cautioned that the more the international community got involved, "the longer, harder and more complicated it will be."
The United States and other Western governments have supported the opposition and cautioned against the use of force.
NATO on Tuesday "strongly deplored" the Serbian government's cancellation of local election results and called on Milosevic to reverse the decision.

"We are dismayed that the Serbian authorities have ignored the calls of the international community to respect internationally recognised democratic principles," the 16 NATO members said in a statement.

In a separate statement, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, also in Brussels, warned if Milosevic wanted to "rule Serbia as an unreformed dictatorship, it will only increase his isolation and the suffering of his people".
The remark was read as a clear hint that Washington could back the reimposition of U.N. sanctions imposed on Yugoslavia for 3-1/2 years during the war in Bosnia.
